options: "742abc" returns 742, because Number() reads the leading digits the way parseInt does
"0x2E6" returns 742: Number() also parses hexadecimal, and 742 passes both checks
" " returns 0, because Number(" ") is 0 and the trim check is skipped
"7.5" returns 7, because the value is truncated to a whole number first
0B-d1/h4.why: Number() accepts hex (0x), binary (0b) and exponent forms, so "0x2E6" and "7.42e2" both become 742. Pydantic's int would reject both strings. " " never gets to Number() because the trim check throws first. Number("742abc") is NaN; only parseInt reads leading digits. "7.5" fails the isInteger check. If you need exactly the same rules in both languages, check the string with a regex such as /^\d+$/.

options: A TypeError at JSON.parse, because "home-equity" isn't a valid loanType
69010 home-equity: creditScore is still the string "690", so + concatenates
Nothing: node reports the type mismatch before running the file
700 home-equity: the number annotation converts "690" on assignment
0B-d2/h4.why: JSON.parse returns any, so the annotation is just a promise to the checker. The types are erased and nothing is checked at run time. creditScore is still the string "690", and "690" + 10 concatenates to "69010". node strips types without checking them. Use tsc --noEmit to type-check your code, and write parse functions for data that comes from outside.

options: cities is ["Plano", undefined, "Boston"]: fetch resolves a 404 to undefined
cities is ["Plano", null, "Boston"]: the as cast fills missing fields with null
Promise.all rejects with a TypeError from data.places[0]; no cities are returned
fetch rejects with an HTTP 404 error, so Promise.all rejects with that
0B-d3/h4.why: fetch only rejects on network failures. A 404 is a normal response with resp.ok set to false. The as cast checks nothing, so data.places is undefined and indexing it throws. Promise.all rejects as soon as one promise does. Check resp.status or resp.ok first, and use Promise.allSettled when partial results are useful, the way return_exceptions is in Python.

options: Both return NaN, which the negative-number check lets through
Both return 0: Number() turns empty and blank strings into 0
Both throw: Number("") is NaN, which the isNaN check catches
"" throws as NaN, but " " returns 0 after trimming
0B-weekly/w12.why: Number("") and Number(" ") are both 0 (Number(null) is also 0), so this validator turns missing data into a plausible-looking value. Pydantic's float rejects "". This is why parseCreditScore checks raw.trim() === "" before converting.
